subject: Biology
title: Giant Sequoias and Redwoods
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Giant Sequoias and Redwoods.

hook.text: The tallest living thing on Earth is a coast redwood named Hyperion, standing 115 meters tall.

buildup.text: Giant sequoias are the largest by volume. General Sherman weighs an estimated 1,900 metric tons.

discovery.text: Their thick bark—up to 60 centimeters—protects them from fire that kills competing trees.

twist.text: Sequoias actually need fire to reproduce. Heat opens their cones and clears the forest floor for seedlings.

climax.text: These giants have survived ice ages and human logging, but climate change now threatens their fog-dependent habitat.

punchline.text: The biggest living things need fire to be born.

quiz.question: How tall is Hyperion, the tallest known tree?

details.summary: Giant sequoias are the world's largest trees by volume, while coastal redwoods are the tallest, exceeding 115 meters. These ancient conifers can live over 3,000 years, their fire-resistant bark and enormous size making them living monuments to the power of time and adaptation.
details.whyItMatters: These ancient trees are irreplaceable ecological treasures that store massive amounts of carbon. Their survival demonstrates forest resilience, while their vulnerability to climate change and wildfires highlights conservation urgency.
takeaways: Giant sequoias can weigh over 1,800 metric tons as the largest living organisms
Coastal redwoods exceed 115 meters, the tallest trees on Earth
Their bark can be over 60 centimeters thick providing fire resistance

faq.question: How do sequoias grow so large and live so long?
faq.answer: Thick bark resists fire and insects. Tannin-rich wood repels decay organisms. They grow in sheltered groves with reliable water. Their size deters most threats. Favorable genetics and the right environment combine to allow millennia of continuous growth.

faq.question: Are giant sequoias threatened by climate change?
faq.answer: Yes. Hotter, drier conditions increase fire severity beyond what even thick bark can withstand. The 2020 and 2021 California wildfires killed thousands of large sequoias. Drought stress weakens their defenses against bark beetles and disease.
